source: Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir, Narayanan (2024) AI Agents That Matter (HumanEval reproduction of LATS)
finding: Independent re-run of the public LATS code on HumanEval, five runs each. LATS with GPT-4 scored below its published figure and cost far more than simple retry baselines with equal or better accuracy.
numbers: Table A1 (164 problems, 5 runs, mean with min-max): LATS GPT-4 88.0 (82.3-91.5) at $134.50; LATS GPT-3.5 80.4 (78.7-83.5) at $9.49; GPT-3.5 zero-shot 73.9 at $0.05; Warming GPT-4 93.2 (92.1-93.9) at $2.45; Retry GPT-4 92.0 at $2.51; Escalation 85.0 at $0.27; Reflexion GPT-4 87.8 at $3.90. LATS paper reports 92.7 (GPT-4) and 83.8 (GPT-3.5).
limits: Authors set iterations 8, expansion 3 after correspondence with LATS authors. Uses April 2024 GPT-4 turbo, not the models in the LATS paper. HumanEval only; the test signal is the example tests.
agent_relevance: LATS GPT-4 is about 55x the cost of the warming baseline for lower mean accuracy. A tree is not shown to beat retries at equal dollars on code with real tests. Closes gap 9 in part: a failed replication exists for HumanEval; none found for HotPotQA.

source: Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir, Narayanan (2024) AI Agents That Matter (evaluation flaws in LATS)
finding: The audit found the LATS HumanEval evaluation was not the standard benchmark: problems removed, only part of the tests used, and some wrong solutions counted as correct.
numbers: LATS and Reflexion removed the 3 of 164 HumanEval problems with no example tests; LATS removed a 4th for an execution error (author reply). LATS evaluated on a subset of the provided test cases. Both LATS and STeP 'marked some incorrectly completed tasks as correct'. Authors said they would update the manuscript.
limits: Based on author correspondence and code reading, not a full re-grading. Scale of the inflation was not quantified in points.
agent_relevance: The 94.4 to 92.7 drop between LATS versions and the 88.0 re-run both point the same way: treat 83.8/92.7 as upper bounds. Our own tests must grade on the full hidden test set.

source: Kapoor, Stroebl, Siegel, Nadgir, Narayanan (2024) AI Agents That Matter (Reflexion vs temperature warming)
finding: A reflect-and-retry loop (Reflexion) did not beat simple temperature-raising retries on HumanEval, and cost more.
numbers: Reflexion GPT-4 87.8 (86.0-90.9) at $3.90 vs Warming 93.2 at $2.45 and Retry 92.0 at $2.51; LDB variants 88.9 to 93.3 at $0.63 to $7.26. Paper states Reflexion and LDB 'cost over 50% more than the warming strategy'.
limits: One benchmark, GPT-4 turbo. Reflexion published figure is 91.0 on 161 problems; the re-run used the 164-problem LDB version.
agent_relevance: Written reflections are not clearly worth their tokens when a real test is the signal. Bears on gap 6 and on S6: include a plain resample arm.

source: Koh, McAleer, Fried, Salakhutdinov (2024/2025) Tree Search for Language Model Agents (best-of-n control)
finding: On a 200-task VisualWebArena subset the authors compared their search with sampling n full trajectories and re-ranking them by the same value function. Search won at about equal LM calls.
numbers: Re-ranking plateaued near 7 runs at about 30% success. Search c=5 beats it, and c=20 reaches 37.0% (no search 24.5%). 'For c=5 and n=5 ... approximately equal inference compute.'
limits: Equal compute is approximate and counts LM calls, not tokens. Single run, no confidence interval printed. GPT-4o, web tasks where no oracle is available.
agent_relevance: Best evidence in this set that a tree beats best-of-N with the same prompted verifier on a real environment (partly answers gap 1: yes on web tasks, with a modest margin; code with tests stays open).

source: Koh et al. (2025) Tree Search for LM Agents (value function ablation)
finding: Value quality sets the gain. Self-consistency on the value (several samples averaged) helped, and a ground-truth reward was best.
numbers: VWA subset success: no search 24.5; LLaVA-34B value with SC n=20 30.0; GPT-4o value no SC 28.5; GPT-4o SC n=5 32.5; GPT-4o SC n=20 37.0; ground-truth reward 43.5.
limits: Value samples were added on top of fixed branching, so this is not a cost-matched test against spending the same calls on more branches. Single run.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gaps 3 and 5: self-consistency on the value is worth about +8.5 points over a single value call (28.5 to 37.0), and a weak judge leaves about 7 points of the 19 available on the table. The cost-matched comparison with extra branches is still missing.

source: Koh et al. (2025) Tree Search for LM Agents (limitations section)
finding: Backtracking in a live web environment was done by resetting and replaying the action list, because the browser Back button loses page state. Destructive actions are excluded.
numbers: Search budget c=20 means up to 20x more LM calls per step. Paper gives order placement as an example of an action that cannot be undone and proposes a destructive-action classifier folded into the value function.
limits: No experiment on destructive tasks; this is a design note. Replay cost grows with depth.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 7 as design guidance: state reversion is simulated by reset-and-replay, and irreversible actions must be gated before expansion. Our schema should mark each operator reversible or not.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) LATS (limitations and appendix B; ablation Table 8)
finding: The paper says LATS needs to revert to earlier states and names HumanEval, WebShop, ALFWorld and ToolBench as environments where that holds. It also says LATS benefits from ground-truth feedback on HotPotQA and gives no ablation without it.
numbers: Table 8 (HotPotQA EM, n=5, k=50): ToT 0.39, RAP 0.54, LATS no LM heuristic 0.37, DFS 0.42, no reflection 0.58, full 0.63. No row removes the ground-truth signal.
limits: Re-read this session. Table text extraction is column-shifted but the Table 8 row values were clear.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open for LATS itself: no author run without the oracle exists. Gap 7: the authors concede rollbacks are not universal.

source: Karthikeyan, Yuan, Mansimov et al. (2025) A Study on Leveraging Search and Self-Feedback for Agent Reasoning (GSM8K)
finding: MCTSr on GSM8K gains a lot only when ground truth picks the answer. With the model's own reward, picking the top-scored node was no better than picking a random node. Majority vote over tree nodes worked best.
numbers: GSM8K accuracy (Llama3-70B / Mistral-7B / Haiku3 / Sonnet3): no search .813/.426/.866/.757; MCTS with ground truth .958/.820/.964/.923; random node .751/.450/.864/.680; majority vote .883/.608/.905/.786; max self-reward .776/.469/.854/.685. 10 MCTS iterations.
limits: One math benchmark, 2024 models, MCTSr (self-refine) not LATS. Single run per cell in Table 1.
agent_relevance: Quantifies gap 2 by proxy: removing the oracle removes most of the gain; on Sonnet3 and Haiku3 self-reward selection scored at or below random. Majority vote over the tree is the safe no-oracle readout for S6.

source: Karthikeyan et al. (2025) Search and Self-Feedback (ToolTalk)
finding: On a multi-turn tool-calling task, MCTS guided by self-feedback made results worse for both models tested.
numbers: ToolTalk F1, 5 runs (F1 computed from the printed precision and recall): Sonnet3 no search 0.706 vs MCTS 0.559 (precision .656 to .502, recall .765 to .630); Haiku3 0.638 vs 0.605 (precision .588 to .567, recall .698 to .648).
limits: Two Claude 3 models only. Row assignment inferred from the garbled table. Authors then add in-context examples and a verifier module to repair feedback; those repairs are not reported here.
agent_relevance: A prompted judge on an open-ended agent task can be below break-even (gap 3): the sign of the effect flipped to negative. Pair any S6 tree with a task-specific check.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally (difficulty-bin analysis)
finding: Beam search beats best-of-N on hard questions and loses on easy ones at larger budgets. Choosing the strategy per difficulty bin matched best-of-N with up to 4x less compute, but the difficulty estimate was expensive.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S*, PRM. Compute-optimal search beats best-of-N 'using up to 4x less test-time compute (e.g. 16 versus 64 generations)'. Model-predicted difficulty used 2048 samples per question scored by the verifier; this cost was not counted. Benefit shrinks at high budget with predicted bins.
limits: Needs a trained PRM. Authors say the estimation cost 'would be problematic' in production.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: gating is workable in principle, but the one measured estimator is far too costly. A prompted cheap difficulty guess has no measured accuracy in this paper.

source: Li (2025/2026) Chain-in-Tree: Back to Sequential Reasoning in LLM Tree Search
finding: A prompted yes/no 'is branching needed here' check (BN-DP) cut runtime 75-85% in three tree-search frameworks with little accuracy change. The self-consistency version was unstable in some settings.
numbers: 14 settings: GSM8K and Math500, Qwen3-32B and LLaMA3-8B, ToT-BS, ReST-MCTS, RAP. BN-DP: 75-85% fewer tokens, calls and time. BN-SC: up to 80% savings but unstable in 1-4 of 14 settings (a few examples with very long steps).
limits: Math only. Gate is per step, not per item. Paper stresses the result depends on BN evaluator accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a prompted, per-step branching gate is cheap and works on math. Not tested on code or web agents. Candidate for an S6 pre-check.

source: Gao et al. (2026) Domain-Specialized Tree of Thought through Plug-and-Play Predictors
finding: A small trained predictor decides when to prune or expand ToT. Accuracy stays level or rises while tokens fall.
numbers: Token cost versus CoT: ToT about 10x, DST 1.5x-2x (figure 1 of the paper). Backbones Qwen3-8B, Llama3.1-8B, Gemma3-12B on GSM8K, SVAMP, GPQA, BBEH. Dropping a predictor component costs 2-7 points.
limits: Predictor is trained per task, so it breaks the no-training rule. Transfer across models and datasets reported only for math.
agent_relevance: Contrast case for gap 8: gating works better with a trained gate than a prompted one; our scaffold has only the prompted route.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025/2026) DeepSeek-R1, appendix on unsuccessful attempts and Appendix E
finding: The R1 team tried MCTS with a value model for self-improvement and gave it up: search space too large, value model too hard to train. They still say MCTS can add to long reasoning at inference.
numbers: AIME 2024 pass@1 79.8, pass@64 90.0; majority voting raised it to 86.7. They write MCTS with a pre-trained value model 'can improve performance during inference' but self-search iteration 'remains a significant challenge'.
limits: No MCTS-on-R1 number is given, only the claim. Text says R1 allocates compute by problem difficulty natively.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: no direct measurement of a tree on a reasoning model here. The native long chain already spends more tokens on hard items, which is the same job a difficulty gate does.

source: Wang, Chen, Li, Chalamala, Liu (2026) Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
finding: With a verifier that scores every attempt, best-of-N over agents saturates fast and one big team stops improving; many small teams in parallel do better. A frontier model had a flat best-of-N curve.
numbers: 12 long-horizon tasks, 27B model, budget 100 agents: teams of 10 beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and one team of 100 on all 4 tasks tested. At 20 agents each task already had 60-94% of the gain of 100 agents. 10-to-20 agents: +1.27% per agent for teams vs +0.64% for parallel agents.
limits: Not tree search; teams of collaborating agents. Tasks include GPU kernels and formal proofs with exact verifiers. Authors' own statistical model.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 4 by analogy: with a hard verifier, plain resampling saturates early and a stronger base model leaves little variance to harvest. Structure that raises the mean per sample matters more than more samples.

source: Aphale and Singh (2026) Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents
finding: Execution-feedback retry beat plain resampling, but fixed task guidance and feedback from other episodes did as well. The gain came from reusable guidance, not from matching the failure.
numbers: 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, 5 retries: template feedback 85.3% vs resample 68.3% (+17.1 pp, 95% CI +9.9 to +24.2). Fixed task template 86.1%, different-label feedback 86.1%. Under token caps: +15.9 pp at 2,000 tokens, +14.7 at 5,000. Nut insertion: feedback 82.5% vs resample 97.5% (n=40).
limits: Simulated robot manipulation, a 7B coder model, confidence intervals too wide to prove equivalence. Not a tree.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: written feedback inside retries may act as static hints, and can hurt when the hint is wrong. Include a fixed-hint arm and a plain resample arm when testing reflection in S6.

source: Aggarwal, Kamal, Japesh et al. (2025) DARS: Dynamic Action Re-Sampling
finding: A depth-first, branch-at-key-steps coding agent reached 47% on SWE-Bench Lite, and the paper's table compares its cost scaling to SWE-Search and to large-sample resampling.
numbers: Table 4: cost scaling factor SWE-Search 14.00 vs DARS 7.60 (GPT-4o, 5 attempts); Large Language Monkeys 250 attempts, single rollout 15.9, coverage 56. Table 5 GPT-4o: SWE-Agent 16.33 ($0.05) to DARS 37.0 ($7.92); Claude 3.5 Sonnet V2: 18.33 to 47 ($12.24).
limits: Text-extracted tables are column-shifted; cost column assignments are my best reading. Authors' own comparison, single run, uses a trained trajectory selector.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: resampling with a real checker is a strong rival on coverage but costs far more per point, and branching only at key steps halves the cost scale versus SWE-Search. No equal-token test against best-of-N with the same selector.

source: Xie et al. (2026) PRISM-MCTS (Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507, reasoning-era backbone)
finding: On a 2025 reasoning-style model, MCTS-style methods gave a mixed picture: big gains on retrieval-heavy GPQA, small ones on math, and one MCTS baseline fell far below zero-shot.
numbers: Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507, rows read by position: GPQA-Diamond EM zero-shot 47.55, MCTS-RAG 64.65, PRISM-MCTS 65.08; MATH500 79.25, 80.60, 82.09; AIME25 48.67, 50.00, 53.33; ReST-MCTS MATH500 70.90, AIME25 20.00. PRISM cut trajectories 18.76 to 8.40 versus MCTS-RAG.
limits: Table text is garbled; row-to-method mapping is inferred from order and the text, so treat as approximate. Gains mix retrieval and search. Authors' own method, no seeds. First-author name not checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: on a modern model the search gain on math is about +1 to +5 points and a poorly tuned tree can lose badly. Strengthens the case for a difficulty gate and an off switch.

source: Choi, Kim, Ong et al. (2026) ReAcTree: Hierarchical LLM Agent Trees with Control Flow
finding: A program-owned tree whose control-flow nodes call the model only for subgoals let a 7B or 8B model beat flat ReAct with 70B-class models. At 7B it lost when the in-context example was complex.
numbers: WAH-NL: Qwen2.5-72B GSR 61% vs ReAct 31% (SSR 54.05 to 79.58). ReAcTree+WM 8B about equals ReAct+WM 70B and is faster; same-size 70B gain +25 pp GSR. 7B ReAcTree under ReAct when memory example missing; 72B reverses it (+18 pp no memory, +29 pp WM only).
limits: Hierarchical task tree, not MCTS; household simulators. Authors' own comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a program-owned control structure with the model as a slot-filler can keep or raise the gain on small models, provided the prompt format stays simple. Supports our design, with a prompt-complexity warning.

source: Yu, Peng, Vajipey et al. (2025) Exact / R-MCTS: Teaching AI Agents to Explore with Reflective-MCTS
finding: Reflective MCTS with a multi-agent debate value function lifted GPT-4o on VisualWebArena by 6% to 30% relative over earlier search agents, at several times the tokens of ReAct. Fine-tuning on the search trees kept 87% of the gain with less compute.
numbers: Table 2 shows token multiples about 3x-5x for ToT/search agent/MCTS and 6x-10x for R-MCTS versus ReAct (column alignment uncertain). Fine-tuned model matches 87% of R-MCTS (abstract).
limits: Table text is column-shifted; success cells not used. Needs weight updates for the 87% result, not allowed for our agent.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 9: a second group builds on the web-search lineage with GPT-4o and sees gains, at high token cost. Not a replication of LATS numbers.
